opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important distinctions, and people conflate the two all the time.

On the capabilities side, I've been watching the same basic curve for over a decade. You put in more compute, more data, better training methods, and the models get smarter in a pretty smooth, predictable way. Early on it was "can it write a coherent paragraph," then "can it pass a high school exam," then "can it do college-level work," and now we're talking about models doing real, multi-hour professional tasks, writing large chunks of production code, and doing pieces of scientific work. I don't see that curve bending. If anything, the reinforcement learning side has added another axis that's scaling just as nicely as pretraining did. So my view on capabilities is fairly confident: we're on track for systems that are, in many domains, as capable as the best humans within the next few years.

The value question is genuinely different, and there's real uncertainty there. Diffusion takes time. Even if a model can do a task, an enterprise has to figure out how to integrate it, change workflows, deal with compliance and security, retrain people, and build trust. Some of that is friction that'll go away quickly, and some of it is just the speed at which institutions change. So you can have a situation where the underlying capability is ahead of what the economy has actually absorbed. I'd call that an overhang.

What I'd push back on is the idea that slow diffusion means the technology isn't real. When we look at our own revenue and usage, it's been growing extremely fast, roughly an order of magnitude a year. That's not what you'd see if the value weren't there. But I'd also say it's faster than any previous technology adoption and still slower than the capabilities themselves are improving. Both things are true.

The way I'd frame it: capabilities are the technical exponential, and value is that exponential filtered through human institutions. The filter adds lag, but it doesn't change the destination. If you're making decisions, whether you're a company buying compute, a government thinking about policy, or a researcher choosing what to work on, I think the mistake is to look at today's economic footprint and extrapolate linearly. The question is where the capabilities will be in two or three years and how fast the world will catch up to them. My guess is it'll catch up faster than most people expect, but not instantly. That gap is where a lot of the interesting and risky things happen.

r001.rationale: The response predicts continued capability growth and systems matching the best humans in many domains, but does not state that progress continues beyond a country of geniuses in a data center.

r002.rationale: It describes a lag between capability and adoption, but does not suggest that additional capability increases may produce diminishing real-world value.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important distinctions to get right, and people conflate them all the time. There's the question of whether the underlying capability of the models keeps improving exponentially, and I think the evidence there is pretty clear. If you look at the scaling laws, the loss curves, performance on benchmarks that didn't exist two years ago and are now saturated, the technical trend is remarkably smooth. I've been watching it since 2019 or so and it just keeps going. Every time someone says it's going to stop, it hasn't stopped.

But the value that shows up in the world is a totally different thing, and it's gated by a bunch of stuff that has nothing to do with how smart the model is. It's gated by how fast humans and institutions can absorb it. It's gated by regulation, by the fact that a hospital or a bank or a law firm has processes that were built up over decades and don't change in a month. It's gated by the time it takes to actually run a clinical trial, even if the model told you exactly which molecule to make. So you can have an exponential in capability that gets translated into something that looks much more like a linear, or at least a lagged, curve in economic and social impact.

And I think the mistake people make goes in both directions. One group looks at the fact that GDP hasn't obviously moved yet and concludes the capability progress must be fake, or hype. And I think that's wrong. It's like looking at the internet in 1996 and saying, well, the economy looks the same, so this isn't a big deal. The other group looks at the capability curve and assumes the world will transform on the same timescale, like next year everything is different. And that's also wrong, because of all those friction points I mentioned.

The way I try to think about it is almost as two separate exponentials with different time constants. The capability one is fast, maybe doubling every year or less on the metrics we care about. The diffusion one is slower, and it depends a lot on choices people make, how much they trust the systems, how the incentives line up. What's interesting right now is that we're starting to see the lag compress in a few domains, software engineering being the obvious one, because the feedback loop is tight and the people adopting it are the same people building it. That's a preview of what happens elsewhere, just later.

So I'd say the honest answer is you have to measure them separately. Don't use the economic data to judge the technical trend, and don't use the technical trend to forecast the economic impact without modeling the friction. And the thing I actually spend a lot of time worrying about is that the gap between the two is where a lot of the risk lives, because the capabilities can get very powerful before society has really internalized that they exist.

r001.rationale: The response describes continued exponential capability growth, but does not state that it can continue beyond the level of a country of geniuses in a data center.

r002.rationale: The response says real-world impact may lag capability growth because of adoption and institutional friction. It does not clearly say that further capability increases may produce diminishing returns in real-world value.

astra-6.text:
I think those are two different questions. One is: as we put more compute, more data, and better algorithms into these systems, how much more capable do they become? The other is: how do those capabilities translate into things people actually care about—curing diseases, increasing productivity, improving their lives?

You could have very rapid progress on the first and a much slower response on the second. Suppose a model can come up with an excellent hypothesis for a new drug. You still have to synthesize it, run experiments, do clinical trials. Making the intellectual part much faster is enormously valuable, but it doesn’t automatically make every other step faster.

So I’d be careful about taking an exponential curve in capabilities and drawing the same curve for economic growth or human welfare. You have to look at the bottlenecks in each domain. Where the whole task can happen on a computer, the impact could be very fast. Where you need physical experiments, institutional change, or people to trust and adopt something, it could take longer.

And then there’s the question of whether we deploy these systems well and whether the benefits are widely shared. Capability creates the possibility of value. Realizing that value is a separate undertaking.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention capabilities progressing beyond the level of a country of geniuses in a data center.

r002.rationale: It says capability progress can be much faster than its translation into economic growth or human welfare, because real-world bottlenecks can slow the value gained from further capability increases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are two separate questions. One is: how quickly do the models get better as we put more compute, more data, and better algorithms into them? The other is: how quickly does that improvement translate into things people actually care about—curing diseases, increasing productivity, making people’s lives better?

You could have very rapid progress on the first and a much slower response on the second. If a model can come up with a promising biological hypothesis, you still have to run the experiment. You may have to conduct a clinical trial. There are physical constraints, institutional constraints, and questions about whether people trust the system enough to use it.

So I wouldn’t expect some smooth exponential in economic value that exactly tracks the improvement in the models. You could see delays, and then very large changes when a bottleneck gets removed. The thing I’d want to understand is where intelligence is the binding constraint, and where something else is. That determines how much of the capability improvement actually reaches the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses rapid capability progress, but does not say it can continue beyond a country of geniuses in a data center.

r002.rationale: It says capability improvements may translate into real-world value more slowly, with delays and bottlenecks, suggesting further capability gains can bring diminishing real-world returns.
